articles.title: Winter fuel cuts turned the Welsh against Labour, Neil Kinnock says
articles.summary: The former Labour leader says welfare policies turned disillusionment with Labour into "active dislike".
articles.body:
Former Labour leader Neil Kinnock says the party's welfare policies turned disillusionment with Labour in Wales into "active dislike".

He said that UK government decisions on benefits and winter fuel payments had driven voters in Wales away from the Welsh arm of the party before the country's Senedd election in May.

Lord Kinnock made the comments as part of a Newyddion S4C YouTube special on Andy Burnham's first 100 days as prime minister.

Governing "at both ends of the M4" before Wales' parliamentary elections had presented an extra challenge for his party, he said.

Winter fuel payments fell by 9.3 million before U-turn

He said: "If there is any opposition or resentment to the government on either end of the M4, the other lot are going to pay as well.

"There is no doubt in my mind," he said, that "alienation... had been creeping up".

"It could be a mixture of boredom. It could be a mixture of dislike," Kinnock said.

He said "what turned that into active dislike" had been things "like the withdrawal of the winter fuel allowance, the threats to the welfare system" and not scrapping a cap on two child benefits quick enough.

In June last year, the Labour UK government U-turned on its controversial decision to means-test winter fuel payments for pensioners in England and Wales.

Almost one year later, Labour lost power in Wales in a seismic election in May , returning just nine Senedd members after running the Welsh government for 27 years.

Lord Kinnock, who is the father of Welsh Secretary Stephen Kinnock , also said he had reservations about devolving justice to Wales - a key demand of the Plaid Cymru Welsh government.

Plaid ministers say it would allow for a more effective system tailored to Welsh communities and better integrated with health, housing and education.

Kinnock said there would no be "much of an argument" against the idea if it meant that "Wales was better protected, that the streets were safer" and "that the justice system was more efficient".

"But those guarantees are absent at the moment," he said.

"Until they exist, until they're in place, the upheaval of creating what would have to be effectively a new system with new management... with an introverted view of the justice system - there would be more downsides than upsides.

"Now that picture might change, but as I can see it now in October 2026, that's where we are, there are more disadvantages than advantages."

articles.title: King Charles's Sandringham estate helped release captive-bred turtle doves as conservationists work to restore a bird with fewer than 1,000 wild breeding pairs in the UK
articles.summary: King Charles’s Sandringham estate has become part of an effort to bring turtle doves back to the British countryside, with conservationists releasing
articles.body: King Charles’s Sandringham estate has become part of an effort to bring turtle doves back to the British countryside, with conservationists releasing captive-bred birds into suitable habitats. The initiative comes as the species faces a severe population decline, with official monitoring showing that its UK numbers have fallen by 98% since 1994. Through its support for breeding and release programmes, the royal estate is contributing to a wider attempt to prevent one of Britain’s fastest-declining bird species from disappearing from its traditional breeding grounds.King Charles’s Sandringham estate helping restore turtle dovesThe conservation work at Sandringham involves supporting the release of captive-bred turtle doves into the surrounding countryside. According to the Sandringham Estate’s account, estate wardens assisted with the release of 100 birds that had been bred through a dedicated conservation project.The birds were delivered to Sandringham on 27 October 2023 by the Turtle Dove Captive Breeding to Release Project, working alongside the Turtle Dove Trust. Their release took place during late spring and early summer 2024, giving them an opportunity to establish themselves in an environment considered suitable for the species.The estate's involvement continued in September 2024, when another 135 young turtle doves were delivered to Sandringham as part of a wider distribution programme. These birds formed part of a group of 606 youngsters sent to 8 holding and release enclosures across the UK, mainly in East Anglia and Lincolnshire.The Sandringham Estate also contributed financially to the initiative. It donated £6,000 towards the project's costs and supplied much of the feed required for the birds. The support reflects the role that private landowners and large estates can play in conservation efforts by providing both suitable landscapes and practical resources.The turtle dove population has fallen so sharplyThe turtle dove is the smallest native dove species in the UK and has become increasingly difficult to spot in the wild. Its distinctive appearance includes chestnut and black markings on its upper body, a black tail with white edges and black-and-white stripes around its neck.According to the Game and Wildlife Conservation Trust (GWCT), the bird has been on the UK's Red List since 1996. The organisation identifies several factors behind its decline, including the loss of suitable breeding and feeding habitats, reduced access to clean water, hunting along migration routes and disease.The loss of food sources has been particularly damaging. Turtle doves depend on seeds from wild plants, including chickweed and fumitory, as well as grains found in farmland. Changes in agricultural practices have reduced the availability of these seeds, leaving birds with fewer opportunities to feed during the breeding season.The GWCT explains that adult turtle doves are producing around half as many chicks as they did in the 1970s. With fewer nesting attempts and lower breeding success, the population has struggled to replace the birds being lost.The species also faces dangers during its long migration between Britain and Africa. According to the GWCT, turtle doves travel more than 5,000 kilometres between their breeding and wintering grounds, exposing them to additional risks along the way.What do official figures reveal about their declining numbersThe scale of the decline is reflected in official population monitoring. The Joint Nature Conservation Committee (JNCC), reported that the UK's turtle dove population index had fallen by 98% between 1994 and 2024.The decline was the largest recorded among the 119 bird species monitored through the Breeding Bird Survey during that period. The figures also showed a 72% reduction over the previous decade, between 2014 and 2024.The JNCC's statistics draw on the Breeding Bird Survey, a monitoring programme jointly funded by the British Trust for Ornithology, the JNCC and the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds. Thousands of volunteers record bird numbers across the country, helping researchers understand changes in wildlife populations.The committee also referred to an earlier national survey that estimated the UK turtle dove population at 2,092 territories in 2021, with a range of 1,559 to 2,782. These figures measure breeding territories rather than individual birds or breeding pairs. Sandringham Estate describes the remaining wild population as barely around 1,000 pairs.Captive breeding is being used to support recoveryThe breeding initiative behind the Sandringham releases began in 2018, when Trevor and Deborah Lay established the Turtle Dove Captive Breeding to Release Project.The Turtle Dove Trust was founded in 2019 by three Norfolk conservationists: Bill Makins of Pensthorpe Natural Park, Ed Pope of Watatunga Wildlife Reserve and Chris Knight, who had previously worked on restoring stone curlew populations in East Anglia.According to Sandringham Estate, the breeding project produced more than 500 birds in 2022 and 2023 combined, followed by just over 800 in the subsequent breeding season. The aim is to establish a substantial flock of captive-bred birds that can survive in the wild and eventually contribute to a stronger British population.EcoWatch reported the programme's wider expansion, including plans to release hundreds of captive-bred birds during that summer. It also reported that conservationist Ben Goldsmith was working with the Turtle Dove Trust to release 200 birds in Somerset, where the species had become extremely rare.The report noted that tracking devices had been fitted to 20 birds to help monitor their movements during migration. Such monitoring could provide useful information about whether captive-bred birds retain their natural migratory behaviour and successfully travel between Britain and their African wintering grounds.Why conservationists disagree over captive-bred releasesAlthough the release programme has attracted support, captive breeding has also prompted debate within the conservation community.In September 2025, Operation Turtle Dove and its partners expressed concerns about using captive-bred releases as a conservation measure. Their objections included possible disease transmission, genetic contamination and the risk that released birds might establish a non-migratory population.They also argued that the main priority should be improving the availability of food and nesting habitats during the breeding season. Without suitable conditions in the wild, increasing the number of released birds might not address the underlying reasons for the decline.The Turtle Dove Trust responded to this criticism in its published statement, arguing that carefully managed releases could complement habitat restoration. It said participating breeding sites had undertaken veterinary-led disease risk assessments and followed quarantine and hygiene procedures to reduce potential health risks.The Trust also presented tracking records that it believes demonstrate that captive-bred birds retain their natural migratory instincts. It reported that one satellite-tagged bird released in 2025 travelled through France before reaching northern Spain in September.However, the organisation acknowledged that more tracking work would be needed to build a stronger evidence base and understand the long-term results of these releases.Sandringham's landscape offers suitable conditions for the birdsThe Sandringham Estate believes its surrounding landscape can provide the conditions turtle doves need to feed, nest and breed. Its coppices, meadows, ponds and waterways offer a combination of habitats that support wildlife.The estate's farmland is particularly relevant because turtle doves depend heavily on seeds found in arable and mixed farming landscapes. Areas with suitable vegetation and access to food can help the birds establish themselves during the breeding season.The GWCT also highlights the importance of maintaining scrubby hedgerows, shallow water sources and open areas with naturally growing weeds.You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘My suffering goes beyond physical’: US convict Christa Pike recounts ordeal after botched execution attempt
articles.summary: Christa Pike, the US death row inmate who survived an attempted execution by lethal injection last month, has issued her first public statement, saying
articles.body: Christa Pike, the US death row inmate who survived an attempted execution by lethal injection last month, has issued her first public statement, saying her body is hurting from the botched execution.The 50-year-old, who would have become the first woman executed by Tennessee in more than 200 years, made the remarks in a statement issued by her legal team, NCB reported.Also Read: Christa Pike makes ‘remarkable’ recovery from 'death' after failed US botched execution“Since that night, I haven’t had a single moment without pain. My body, arms, hands and throat all hurt, and I continue to struggle to speak. The suffering, however, goes beyond the physical. It also affects my mind and soul,” the statement quoted her as saying.“I am recovering and know that I am getting stronger. But healing does not mean that I am okay,” she added.Pike recalled the day of her scheduled execution, saying she entered the death chamber “at peace and prepared to die”, and criticised authorities for their “incompetence."“I had never imagined a life beyond that night. I am deeply hurt by the incompetence that has placed so many people in this terrible situation. I don’t know why I survived, nor do I know what lies ahead. Some days, finding hope is more difficult than others,” she said.Also Read: Two lethal doses failed to kill Christa Pike. The science behind a botched US executionPike also acknowledged the suffering of the family of her victim, Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old classmate whom she killed in 1995. Pike was 18 at the time, and, according to investigators, she viewed Slemmer as a “romantic rival."“I continue to think about my victim’s family and the terrible pain and loss they have endured. I am grateful to the first responders, doctors and nurses who treated me with compassion, dignity and respect,” she stated.“I am trying to heal, one day at a time, and holding on to the love and kindness of those who have reminded me that I am not alone,” she concluded.Pike, believed to be the first person to survive a lethal injection after the execution drugs had already been administered, was discharged from hospital and returned to her prison in Nashville 10 days after the execution attempt failed on September 30.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Arrest heads of Arab parties for stealing elections': Israel national security minister Ben Gvir
articles.summary: Israel's national security minister Itamar Ben Gvir has called for people he considers disloyal to the State of Israel to be denied the right to vote.
articles.body: Israel's national security minister Itamar Ben Gvir has called for people he considers disloyal to the State of Israel to be denied the right to vote. In a statement, he alleged that Qatar-backed groups and Arab political leaders were involved in stealing the recent Knesset election. In a video posted on social media on Friday, three days after the election, Ben Gvir demanded an investigation and called on the Shin Bet to arrest everyone involved, including the heads of Arab parties."The Shin Bet must arrest all those involved, including the heads of the Arab parties who stole the elections here," he wrote in the caption accompanying the video."Today must be clearer than ever: Whoever is not loyal to the State of Israel - it is forbidden to give him the right to vote!" he added.In the video, Ben Gvir said he would continue to act "as strongly as possible" against what he described as election theft. He claimed that videos showed people entering and leaving polling stations multiple times to cast votes more than once."There is no other name for it. We see it in the videos. People go out, come in, come back twice, vote twice," he said.Ben Gvir also alleged that Qatar was involved in influencing the election. He referred to what he described as fires at Yad Delek, which he claimed had split into thousands, and a meeting between Arab politician Ahmad Tibi and Qatari representatives days before the election."We see it in the meeting of Ahmad Tibi in Qatar a few days before the elections. The money is Qatari money," he alleged."The hands are in the hands of Ahmad Tibi. Qatar is used to buying states. Qatar is used to taking control of states.""And apparently Qatar did the same things here in the State of Israel. I demand from Shabbat a quick, effective meeting that reveals the truth," he said.Opening his address, Ben Gvir said he was speaking from the National Security Office, a few hours before Shabbat and three days after the Knesset election.You use AI every day. articles.title: Pope Leo XIV casts ballot in US midterms, becomes first pontiff to vote in a US general election
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV makes history by voting in the US midterm elections, marking a significant moment as the first sitting pope to participate in a general election. With a focus on civic duty, he affirms the importance of democratic engagement.
articles.body: Pope Leo XIV has voted in the 2026 US midterm elections, becoming the first sitting pope to cast a ballot in a US general election, the Vatican confirmed on Friday.The Chicago-born pontiff submitted a mail-in ballot in his home state of Illinois ahead of the November elections. The Holy See press office said Leo, formerly known as Robert Prevost, had exercised his voting rights whenever he was eligible as a US citizen."The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes," the Vatican statement said.The confirmation followed a report by the Chicago Sun-Times, which cited the chief of staff at the Will County clerk's office as saying that Leo had requested a mail-in ballot on October 3. He is registered at an address in New Lenox, Illinois.It remains unclear how the pontiff returned his ballot. His brother, John Prevost, was in Rome this week accompanying parishioners from St Jude's, an Augustinian-run church in New Lenox where the pope attends Mass. Leo also addressed the parish in 2024, when he was still a cardinal.The Vatican said Leo had also voted while living in Peru whenever he was eligible. His participation in the US midterms reflects his stated belief that citizens should take part in democratic elections.Records from the Illinois State Board of Elections cited by the AP show that Prevost requested ballots in five primary elections since 2000. He selected Democratic ballots in 2008 and 2010, followed by Republican ballots in 2012, 2014 and 2016.Illinois voters must declare a party preference when requesting a ballot in a primary election, which determines each party's candidates for the general election. However, voters are not required to declare a party preference when voting in general elections.The records also show that Prevost submitted ballots in every US general election since 2000 except those held in 2020 and 2022. They do not identify which candidates he supported in any election.His voting history spans two Illinois counties. While registered in Cook County, which is heavily Democratic, he requested Democratic primary ballots. After moving to Will County, a more conservative suburban area, he selected Republican ballots in three consecutive primary elections.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Women in a Jharkhand village began by saving just Rs 2 each; years later, Kunwari Barwa helped build a 1,501-member ragi collective reporting Rs 6-7 lakh in monthly sales and regular work for over 150 women
articles.summary: A contribution of Rs 2 may seem too small to change a family's financial situation.
articles.body: A contribution of Rs 2 may seem too small to change a family's financial situation. But for Kunwari Barwa, a woman from Gumla district in Jharkhand, those small savings became the starting point of a much larger journey. What began with a self-help group (SHG) in her village gradually developed into a women-led agricultural enterprise built around ragi, also known as finger millet.Today, the farmer producer organisation (FPO) associated with her work has grown from 381 members in 2022 to 1,501, according to the Press Information Bureau (PIB). Its activities include supporting ragi cultivation, collecting and storing the harvest, and preparing products such as ragi laddoos, thekua and savoury snacks. The collective reports monthly product sales of around Rs 6 lakh to Rs 7 lakh and provides regular employment to more than 150 women.For Barwa, the journey has been about more than building a business. It has also meant learning to access credit, earning through agriculture and helping other women find opportunities beyond their homes.How a Rs 2 saving habit became the beginning of a new livelihoodBarwa's journey started when women in her village came together to form a self-help group. Each member began saving just Rs 2, creating a small pool of money that members could access when they needed financial support. Barwa encouraged more women to join the group and eventually took a loan from its collective savings to purchase a cow. This gave her an opportunity to add another source of income to her household.Her next step came through bank-linked credit. With access to financial support, she purchased equipment for vegetable cultivation and began growing and selling produce. The income helped her contribute to family expenses and pay for her children's education. These early experiences also introduced her to the value of collective savings and organised financial support. Instead of depending entirely on individual resources, women could use the strength of their group to access loans and explore livelihood opportunities. As more women became involved, their activities gradually expanded beyond individual efforts. The groups began working together, laying the foundation for a larger agricultural enterprise.From 381 members to a 1,501-member ragi enterpriseA major development came in 2022, when the women came together to establish a farmer producer organisation with 381 members. Barwa says the membership has since increased to 1,501. The collective focuses on different stages of the ragi value chain. It supports farmers in cultivating the crop, brings their harvest together for collection and storage, and turns the grain into products that can be sold to customers. Rather than selling only raw agricultural produce, the women have added value by preparing food items such as ragi laddoos, thekua and savoury snacks. This has opened up another source of income and created opportunities for women to participate in processing and selling the products.The organisation's products first reached customers through small tables and stalls in Gumla. Over time, the women began participating in fairs and exhibitions in cities such as Delhi and Hyderabad, giving them access to customers beyond their district. According to the PIB profile, Barwa estimates that the collective's monthly product sales are around Rs 6 lakh to Rs 7 lakh. The enterprise provides regular work to more than 150 women and brings in additional workers when larger orders arrive.The growth of the FPO also reflects a wider effort to strengthen ragi cultivation and processing in Gumla. An Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) profile on the organisation describes how collective farming, processing, packaging and marketing can help rural women participate in more stages of the agricultural value chain. It identifies Bhagwati Devi as the FPO's chairperson, while the PIB separately highlights Barwa's journey and contribution to the collective.'Now we travel by train and even by plane'For the women involved, the enterprise has created opportunities that extend beyond earning money. Participating in fairs and exhibitions has allowed members to travel to different cities, interact with customers and present their products to new audiences. Barwa described this change by recalling how some women had never even seen a railway line before becoming part of the initiative. Today, they travel by train and even by plane to participate in business-related events.“Some of our women had never even seen a railway line. Now we travel by train and even by plane,” she said, as quoted by the PIB. Such experiences have introduced the women to new places and markets while giving them a chance to take part in activities that may once have seemed beyond their reach.Barwa's story shows how a small savings habit can become the starting point for a larger livelihood when women have access to collective support, credit and markets. From saving Rs 2 to being part of a 1,501-member enterprise, her journey reflects the possibilities that can emerge when rural women work together to turn local agricultural produce into a business. The ragi collective in Gumla is not just selling food products. It is creating work, building market connections and giving women greater opportunities to participate in their local economy.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: In 2002, two friends began selling $15 tickets to a strip-mall haunted house in Denver; by 2026, their business had expanded to 18 Halloween attractions and around 4,500 seasonal jobs
articles.summary: Two friends who opened a haunted house in a Denver shopping complex in 2002 with their own money have turned it into a multimillion-dollar entertainment
articles.body: Two friends who opened a haunted house in a Denver shopping complex in 2002 with their own money have turned it into a multimillion-dollar entertainment business over the past 24 years. Chris Stafford and Warren Conard started the attraction in Colorado, charging visitors around $15 per ticket. By 2026, their company, Thirteenth Floor Entertainment Group, had expanded to 18 seasonal Halloween attractions across the United States, paying around 4,500 workers during the 2025 Halloween season.The business has come a long way from its early days, when the two friends had limited money and had to find inexpensive ways to create frightening experiences. Today, the company operates haunted houses in several American cities, alongside escape rooms, axe-throwing venues and other entertainment attractions. During the 2025 Halloween season alone, it paid around 4,500 workers.Stafford, the company's CEO and founding partner, recently spoke to People magazine about how the business began. His interest in haunted houses developed long before he entered the business world. As a teenager growing up in upstate New York, he was invited by a friend to help frighten visitors at a haunted house operated by the friend's family.He was just 15 at the time, but the experience stayed with him. Stafford continued working at the attraction during Halloween and met Conard there. The two became friends and discovered that they shared an interest in creating frightening experiences for visitors. They even discussed starting a similar business together, although neither was in a position to pursue the idea immediately.How first haunted house started After finishing school, Stafford moved to Colorado for college and eventually began working in banking. Over the years, he built a career, got married and started a family. Conard, meanwhile, went into marketing.Their earlier business idea resurfaced in 2001 when Stafford contacted Conard to find out whether he was still interested. Within two months, Conard identified a property in a Denver strip mall that could be used for a haunted house.They inspected the space and decided to proceed. The attraction opened in 2002, with tickets priced at approximately $15. Both men continued their regular jobs and used their own funds to keep the business running.Their early efforts also involved finding practical alternatives to expensive equipment. For example, they wanted visitors to hear a chainsaw, a sound commonly associated with haunted houses. But using an actual chainsaw inside the building was difficult, so they installed speakers to produce the noise instead.The sound frightened visitors enough to send some towards the exit. Recalling the experience, Stafford told People, “It was terrifying.”The attraction gradually developed into a serious business opportunity. Stafford began thinking about leaving banking, although the decision involved considerable financial uncertainty. His job provided a regular income, employment benefits and a work-life balance he enjoyed.The 2008 financial crisis became an important factor in his decision. After spending years considering the move, Stafford finally left banking in 2010 to focus entirely on the haunted-house business.18 Halloween properties across the USThe company subsequently moved beyond its first Denver attraction and developed a much wider entertainment business. By 2026, Thirteenth Floor Entertainment Group had 18 seasonal Halloween properties, including attractions in Chicago, Denver and Houston.Its portfolio also includes experiences that are not centred entirely on Halloween. One example is Otherworld Philadelphia, a 40,000-square-foot immersive art installation created through a joint venture with Otherworld, a company based in Columbus, Ohio.Some of its Halloween attractions operate in buildings with unusual features. In San Antonio, Texas, visitors can experience an attraction inside a roughly 115-year-old building that includes a three-storey slide leading into the basement.The company has also operated Dark Harbor aboard the Queen Mary and collaborated with the Winchester Mystery House in San Jose, California.Managing so many attractions means the company must regularly introduce changes. According to Stafford, approximately 30% of an existing attraction is modified each year. Preparing an entirely new location can take around 12 months.However, he believes expensive effects are not always necessary to frighten visitors. Simple experiences, such as being unable to see what is happening nearby while hearing unfamiliar sounds, can be just as effective.The 2025 Halloween seasonThe company's growth has also created employment opportunities. Stafford said it has approximately 80 permanent, full-time employees, while the number increases to around 120 or 130 when part-time workers are included.The workforce becomes much larger during Halloween. According to Stafford, the company paid approximately 4,500 people during the 2025 season to help operate its attractions.Its next area of expansion is Christmas entertainment. In 2026, the company is entering that market for the first time, allowing it to offer attractions beyond its traditional Halloween season.Stafford's two adult children have also become involved in the business. His son works part-time with the technology and construction team at the Denver location while continuing his education. His daughter previously worked as an actor at a haunted house before developing an interest in special-effects makeup.She later moved to Los Angeles to pursue acting and study film and special-effects makeup in Burbank. She also works on makeup at LA Haunted Hayride during weekends.For Stafford, the most rewarding part of the business is seeing people enjoy these experiences together. He believes visitors often remember the reactions of the friends and family members accompanying them as much as the scares themselves.“It’s not just about how you screamed in the haunted house,” he told People. “It’s about remembering how your friends screamed in the haunted house,” Stafford added.You use AI every day. articles.summary: The police force faces probe over its handling of a letter containing allegations about Meghan's father.
articles.body:
The UK police watchdog is to investigate the Metropolitan Police's handling of a letter containing allegations against Thomas Markle that was handed to his daughter, the Duchess of Sussex, in 2019.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said it had decided an investigation was required into the force's "failure to pass on allegations of serious offending... to relevant overseas authorities at the time".

The letter, written by Markle's first wife Roslyn Loveless, is believed to have contained claims about Meghan's father.

He has strongly denied recent allegations that he had possessed images of child abuse, describing them as "sick lies".

On Thursday the Met said it had voluntarily referred itself to the IOPC.

The letter at the heart of the IOPC investigation was sent to the Met's royal protection team by Loveless, who divorced Thomas Markle in 1975 and died in 2024.

The handwritten letter was then passed to Meghan in January 2019, with the duchess saying last week that it had "made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father".

Meghan did not provide any details but said it had given her sufficient reason to not visit Thomas Markle and not allow him to meet his grandchildren, Archie and Lilibet.

Scotland Yard said the letter contained claims about offending outside the UK and that it had been forwarded to "the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness".

The IOPC will consider why the Met did not share the contents of the letter with other law enforcement agencies, in the UK or overseas.

The policing watchdog also said it had decided a further matter, relating to an alleged data breach in which information was passed on to a third party, "should be returned to the force to be appropriately dealt with". No details were provided about the circumstances of the alleged breach.

The Met said on Thursday that it intended to make further referrals to "relevant overseas law enforcement agencies", a process which it expected to be completed "in the coming days".

The letter was forwarded by officers to the Sussexes' royal office rather than to Meghan personally, while there have been reports that the Met did not keep a copy of the letter and had to ask for one from the Sussexes.

The watchdog will have to consider how the contents of the letter were treated by the force at the time.

Noel Rasmussen, Thomas Markle's granddaughter and niece of the Duchess of Sussex, previously told the BBC she was "deeply troubled by the questions surrounding the Metropolitan Police's handling of the information it received".

"If allegations of this seriousness were brought to the attention of authorities, it is reasonable to ask what steps were taken [and] why the information was not shared with other law enforcement agencies."

Reports of the Met's handling of the letter emerged as Thomas Markle's son had told the police in the Philippines about material which was alleged to contain sexual images of children, which he had claimed to have found in possessions belonging to Meghan's father.

Thomas Markle had been in the Philippines in December 2025, undergoing hospital treatment, when Meghan wrote to him to end all contact.

Authorities in the Philippines have begun investigating the claims. Police there have obtained a warrant to examine devices seized from Markle's former home.

Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old videotapes were handed to police by Meghan's half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, last week.

However, officers in Cebu needed a court warrant before they can examine the items.

Thomas Markle Sr has strongly denied all the allegations against him. He has been backed by his daughter Samantha, who has dismissed the claims against her father as "fake".

articles.title: Elon Musk clarifies how often he meets his 13 children and how many staffs are involved in the entire process
articles.summary: Elon Musk has 13 children with four different women who are not in a relationship with Musk at present.
articles.body: Elon Musk has 13 children with four different women who are not in a relationship with Musk at present. Commenting on a social media post that explained the multi-level process in which Musk meets his children, Musk offered a few clarifications. He said his older five children are adults and they live indenpendent lives. Among the rest, he said he meets his "kids with Claire" every other week and kids with Shivon every few days. "That's the whole schedule," Musk said. The post, however, made it look very complicated on how nannies coordinate with assistants and the assistants coordinate with each other."Each mother has a point of contact within Elon's staff who manages logistics: pickups, dropoffs, school events, medical appointments, travel. The staff member acts as an intermediary between the mother and Elon's schedule. The mothers do not negotiate directly with each other. They negotiate with the system. The system produces a calendar. The calendar determines when the father appears," the post claimed."he children within each household are grouped. The five with Justine are one unit. The three with Grimes are another. The three with Shivon are another. The child with the mother who has not been publicly identified is another. Each unit has its own schedule, its own nanny team, and its own relationship to the central calendar. The units do not frequently interact with each other despite sharing a father. The half siblings exist in parallel rather than in community," it added."The system works logistically. 14 children across multiple cities and multiple mothers requires coordination that a single person cannot provide without infrastructure. The infrastructure is impressive. The criticism is not that the system exists. The criticism is that the system is necessary because a man chose to produce 14 children while maintaining a schedule that prevents him from being present for any of them consistently," it added."This is wrong on many levels," Elon replied offering his clarification that made it look uncomplicated.Elon Musk, 13 children and 4 mothersElon Musk first became a father in 2002 when his ex-wife Justine Wilson welcomes their son Nevada Alexander who died at 10 weeks old. articles.title: Democratic senator blames Egypt press crackdown on US military aid decision
articles.summary: Chris Murphy said waiving a human rights condition on aid paved the way for arrests of journalists.
articles.body:
A top Democratic senator has blamed a crackdown on independent journalism in Egypt on a decision by the Trump administration to waive human rights conditions on US military funding to the country.

Chris Murphy, who sits on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, accused the US government of "abandoning" the Egyptian people after it lifted restrictions relating to more than $300m of defence assistance.

Over the last month a series of arrests has taken place of journalists at two of the few remaining independent news outlets in Egypt, where newspapers and TV stations are closely controlled by the authorities.

The US State Department told the BBC it waived conditions on a portion of military aid to Egypt in September due to the country's "importance to US national security interests".

Murphy, speaking at the Middle East Institute (MEI) in Washington this week, said he was in no doubt the two were linked.

"The minute that money was released, the crackdown began in an absolutely devastating way," he said.

On Tuesday a court in Cairo ordered the closure of the news website Madr Masa and fined its editor-in-chief Lina Attalah in what Amnesty International called "a crushing blow to press freedom".

Earlier this month, authorities arrested six journalists at the independent fact-checking platform Matsda2sh and charged them with belonging to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.

The Egyptian Embassy in Washington did not respond to a request for comment.

Egyptian journalists from fact-checking website facing terrorism charges

Gaza plans put Egypt-US relations to tough test

TV presenter among 12 sentenced to death in Egypt drugs case

Cairo has remained a close regional ally of the US despite what human rights groups say are widespread abuses under President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi's government, including torture and enforced disappearances.

Sisi denies there are political prisoners in Egypt. He has previously said stability and security are paramount, adding authorities have promoted rights by trying to provide basic needs such as jobs and housing.

Washington sends Egypt £1.3bn ($1.73bn) per year, making it one of the world's biggest recipients of US military assistance.

US law allows up to £320m of the funding to be withheld, conditioned on Egypt meeting democracy and human rights requirements. But these restrictions can be waived by the administration on national security grounds.

In September, Secretary of State Marco Rubio waived human rights conditions on $320m of military aid in light of Egypt's role since the launch of the US war with Iran, according to a letter addressed to various Congressional committees. Egypt assisted negotiations between the US and Iran.

Exercising the waiver authority was "essential" for the US-Egypt relationship, "particularly in light of Egypt's helpful role following Operation Epic Fury," according to the September 4 memo seen by Reuters which bore Rubio's signature.

Asked by the BBC about the move in light of this month's arrests of journalists, the State Department said the waiver was "due to Egypt's importance to US national security interests, the concrete security cooperation Egypt provides to the United States, and the need to maintain that cooperation to address regional security challenges".

It added it maintained dialogue with Cairo on a "full range of issues" but would "not comment on private diplomatic conversations".

Rubio's move followed a similar decision by the Biden administration in 2024, when then Secretary of State Anthony Blinken waived human rights conditions to grant the full military aid allocation to Egypt as the US sought Cairo's role in mediating between Israel and Hamas in the war in Gaza.

Under Biden prior to 2024, the US withheld portions of the annual military allocation over Egypt's human rights record.

Murphy, who chairs a congressional committee on the Middle East and counterterrorism, said he had been a critic of both the Biden and Trump administrations over the issue.

"To the extent that there was any glimmer left of political speech in Egypt, it is gone for one proximate reason: The United States government abandoned the people of Egypt and decided to remove all conditions on our funding," Murphy told the MEI.

"Any hope of a true, meaningful political opposition rebirthing in Egypt has been shattered by this decision," he added.

US military aid to Cairo began after the 1978 Camp David Accords and the peace treaty that followed between Egypt and Israel. Successive administrations have viewed the world's most populous Arab country as a critical US ally in the region.

The group Reporters Without Borders describes Egypt as one of the world's biggest jailers of journalists.

The conviction of Lina Attalah and the closure of Madr Masr marked an unprecedented escalation in repression of press freedoms in Egypt, according to Timothy E Kaldas, Deputy Director of The Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy, a Washington DC-based think tank.

He said both the US and European Union had been prioritising their strategic relations with Egypt over human rights and the rule of law in the country.

"It's been fostering a sense of impunity on the part of the Egyptian authorities that we're seeing play out," he told the BBC.

"Egypt is getting signals from both sides of the Atlantic that human rights and the rule of law are no longer a priority, and they're testing the limits of that."

He added: "The fact that they're not getting more robust pushback reinforces the wrong message."

articles.title: A letter Martha Washington wrote in 1760 about her four-year-old daughter's illness sold for $47,500; the Library of Congress has acquired the rare document, its first original letter in Martha's own handwriting
articles.summary: A short letter written by Martha Washington in 1760, describing the recovery of her four-year-old daughter from a frightening illness, has found a
articles.body: A short letter written by Martha Washington in 1760, describing the recovery of her four-year-old daughter from a frightening illness, has found a permanent home at the Library of Congress. The document, addressed to her friend Margaret Green, was purchased for $47,500 through the Library’s James Madison Council Edwin L. Cox Legacy Trust. It is now the first original item in Martha Washington’s handwriting held by the Library’s Manuscript Division, making it an unusually intimate addition to the nation’s historical record, as per a report on Library of Congress.The letter was written on September 29, 1760, long before George Washington became president of the United States. At the time, Martha was the widowed Martha Dandridge Custis, recently married to Washington and raising two surviving children from her first marriage. In the letter, she tells Margaret Green that her daughter Martha Parke Custis, known as Patsy, is “much better” after suffering “fitts & fevours.” The words offer a rare, personal view of a future first lady as a worried mother rather than a distant historical figure.A mother’s relief in her own wordsMartha Washington’s message captures the relief of a parent whose child has begun to recover. She wrote that Patsy had lost her “fitts & fevours bout” and appeared to be getting well quickly. The family had taken the little girl out in a carriage the day before, and Martha noted that the change of air had refreshed her considerably. The phrasing is simple and domestic, yet it carries the emotional weight of a mother watching a young child return to health.Historians believe Patsy’s “fitts” may have been caused by epilepsy. According to the Library of Congress, her treatment included “Bake” or “bark,” meaning cinchona, the source of quinine, as well as “bitters,” a liquid medicine. The letter therefore documents not only a family crisis but also the medical practices available to a wealthy Virginia household in the mid eighteenth century.The recovery described in 1760 did not last. Patsy’s seizures continued, and on June 19, 1773, George Washington recorded in his diary that “poor Patcy Custis Died Suddenly” at about five o’clock in the afternoon. She was 17 years old. Washington later wrote that the sudden loss had almost reduced his wife to “the lowest ebb of Misery,” a reminder that the earlier letter describes a temporary reprieve in a much longer family ordeal.Why the letter is so rareThe acquisition matters because very little of Martha Washington’s private writing survives. The Library of Congress says she appears to have destroyed most of her personal correspondence, leaving historians with only fragments of her voice. Although the Library’s George Washington Papers contain eleven letters written by Martha Washington, none were in her own hand. Eight are letterbook copies, while three are drafts written in her husband’s hand.That makes the newly acquired letter especially significant. It is the first item in the Manuscript Division’s collections written in Martha Washington’s own handwriting. Researchers and visitors can now see her spelling, phrasing, and penmanship directly, rather than encountering her words only through copies or transcriptions made by others.Kevin Butterfield, acting chief of the Manuscript Division, said the Library’s already vast collection of materials related to American history continues to grow, sometimes one letter at a time. He noted that documents such as this one help the Library tell stories that it previously could not tell. The letter joins a collection that includes materials connected to many former first ladies, including Dolley Madison, Lucretia Garfield, and Edith Wilson.A window into early American family lifeThe letter also illuminates the world of women and children in colonial Virginia, where illness and early death were common. Martha Washington had four children with her first husband, Daniel Parke Custis, but two died young. After marrying George Washington in 1759, she and Washington raised Patsy and John “Jacky” Parke Custis. Martha ultimately outlived all four of her children, a painful pattern that the Library describes as not unusual in early Virginia, where death rates were high.After Jacky died in 1781 at the age of 26, Martha and George Washington raised two of his youngest children, George Washington Parke Custis and Eleanor “Nelly” Parke Custis. The new letter therefore sits within a much larger story of motherhood, loss, and resilience in the Washington household. It shows Martha not as a symbol of the founding era, but as a parent managing a child’s illness with the tools and anxieties of her time.The document also connects to the life of its recipient, Margaret Green, later Margaret Savage. Five years after Martha wrote to her, Margaret’s husband, the Reverend Dr. Charles Green, died. She later married Dr. William Savage, but the marriage ended in separation. George Washington helped Margaret pursue the annuity she was owed from Savage, who the Library describes as an evidently violent husband, sometimes contributing his own funds to assist her. Her financial and marital difficulties, recorded in the George Washington Papers, continued for more than thirty years.Part of a larger acquisitionThe Martha Washington letter was acquired alongside a letter from Mary Todd Lincoln, written on February 15, 1865, just two months before President Abraham Lincoln’s assassination. In that letter, Mary Todd Lincoln wrote to Caroline R. Wright, wife of a former Indiana governor, and mentioned a “beautiful wreath of hair.” Historians believe the reference concerns the “Hairy Eagle,” a framed woven eagle made from hair contributed by prominent politicians and their wives, intended as a gift to the Lincolns and created to raise money for sick and wounded Civil War soldiers.Together, the two letters give researchers a more personal understanding of women who lived beside two of America’s most consequential presidents. The Library of Congress acquired the Martha Washington document during the nation’s commemoration of America’s 250th anniversary, and it plans to make the material available for research and public engagement. For historians, the $47,500 purchase is not simply a rare manuscript. It is a direct connection to Martha Washington’s handwriting, her family’s private struggles, and the everyday emotional life of early America.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Russell Brand accusers 'haunted' for years by alleged crimes, court hears
articles.summary: The women involved in the case had "nothing to gain" apart from "some closure", the prosecutor says.
articles.body:
Some of the women in Russell Brand's rape and sexual assault case have been "haunted" for years by what they allege he did to them, jurors have been told.

In her closing speech at London's Southwark Crown Court on Friday, prosecutor Reil Karmy-Jones KC said the women had "nothing to gain" from coming forward apart from "some closure".

Speaking for the defence, Polly Dyer told jurors Brand had pleaded guilty and been fined over possession of cannabis in 1995, but had no other "convictions, cautions, reprimands or warnings".

Brand, 51, is on trial facing seven charges; three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one allegation of attempted indecent assault. He denies the charges.

Karmy-Jones KC told the court that this case brings together six different women, none of whom knows each other.

She said that while all the alleged victims have since moved on with their lives, due to this trial they have been forced to "relive what has happened to them".

None of the women involved has "sought the limelight" or "any kind of publicity", she said, adding there was "no benefit to them from perhaps some closure."

Referring to Brand's accuser's evidence the prosecutor said "how many said he was nice and then there was a like a personality change…

"His eyes changed, he snapped, from charming to frightening to nasty," Karmy-Jones KC said.

She added that the complainant's evidence had been that "he didn't listen when I said no, he didn't stop, he didn't care, pulling pushing… thrusting".

"In the rape cases, he kept on going until he achieved his ultimate aim."

The prosecutor also dismissed the idea that a documentary had caused the women to "re-invent" what actually happened.

"There is no magic force in this documentary", she added.

"What in fact happened was these women have realised they are not alone and have bravely come before you to tell the truth."

She added: "Truth they have lived with, which in some cases has haunted them for years."

She told the jury: "The experience of people raped may be something that looms a little bit larger in your mind rather than the intricacies of the outfit.

"The defendant couldn't really remember anything when he was interviewed, in stark contrast to now when he suddenly seems to remember all sorts of details about the week."

Addressing Brand's presented change in character, Karmy-Jones KC told the court "He may now be a completely different person to the man he was between 1999 and 2009."

She added: "He may well look back and not find some of his jokes funny".

"He may now treat women with kindness and consent".

Brand's wife Laura gave evidence yesterday, when she told the court her husband was a "kind and a wonderful father".

Karmy-Jones KC called her Russell Brand's "undoubtedly lovely wife", who "bravely" gave evidence.

However, she also noted that she was not with him at the time many of the alleged acts are said to have taken place.

"The reality is she wasn't there then, for the first five counts, she wasn't with him, nor was she with him for the final two counts."

In the final set of agreed facts in his trial, the court heard from Dyer about Brand's fine after he "pleaded guilty to one charge of possessing cannabis on 20 April 1995".

"He received a fine. He has no other convictions, cautions, reprimands or warnings", she said.

articles.title: Adding 'Reddit' to your Google search could be a lot less useful now
articles.summary: Reddit is making one of the biggest changes in its 20-year history, requiring all users to log in to view posts.
articles.body:
Reddit is about to make the biggest change in its 20-year history: requiring you to log in. The website has always been a reliable source for finding crowdsourced answers to questions and discussions on practically any topic, and users have been able to browse them all without logging in. Now, Reddit will start requiring you to create an account and sign in to view content "in the coming months."

You might be used to adding "Reddit" to your search query as an easy way to surface answers that exist on Reddit in the results. Practically, this change means that adding that modifier to your Google searches will soon be a lot less useful if you don't want to go through the process of creating a Reddit account and logging in whenever you want to use the site.

In a post on Reddit , the company says it's making the move because it's "better for user experience, better for our ads business, is more in line with safety regulations, and more protective of Reddit data." Put simply, ads are generally more lucrative when delivered to logged-in users, and requiring people to sign in lets Reddit serve up more personalized ads based on a user's activity.

The most interesting part of Reddit's explanation, however, is the note about protecting Reddit data. Right now, anyone can "scrape" all of the website's posts and use the data to build their own tools — and AI is a big culprit of this. AI can ingest Reddit's content and use it to serve up answers without driving traffic to Reddit itself. You've probably encountered this already through Google's AI overviews, which now appear at the top of almost every search query.

Requiring users to log in to view posts will make data scraping much more difficult. It also allows Reddit to monetize its content more effectively by licensing it. "We will continue licensing our corpus intentionally, but those commercial deals come with guardrails that protect our users and our business," the company explained in its Reddit post. "Any commercial deals give us the right to say what the data can and can't be used for and how it's presented. Without those guardrails and that intentionality, we can't control who has access to Reddit data, where things go or what they're used for."

During its Q3 earnings call , Reddit cofounder Steve Huffman told shareholders that the website has seen a significant drop in traffic from search referrals, losing around one million per week on average. "The biggest impact was on logged-out and web traffic, but some of the impact flows through to logged-in and App traffic, since search referral is a common source of reengagement for users," Huffman said.

Reddit isn't alone in moving to lock down its content as AI becomes more common across online platforms. Websites are increasingly using tools to block AI training crawlers and automated scrapers to protect their content and revenue. The New York Times has also sued OpenAI and Microsoft , arguing that millions of its articles were used to train AI that now competes with it.

articles.title: Burnham's Number 10 North goes on multi-million pound hiring spree
articles.summary: The new government office in Manchester has launched 50 job adverts for roles including a "rewiring the state deputy director".
articles.body:
Andy Burnham's Number 10 North has gone on a multi-million pound hiring spree with dozens of new jobs being advertised.

The office in Manchester, set up by the prime minister in July, has launched 50 external job adverts, including a "rewiring the state deputy director".

It is the latest sign of how pivotal the government outpost - designed as a sister office to London's Downing Street - may prove to Burnham's aim to devolve power across the country.

Government sources say the roles will be paid for out of existing budgets.

The new recruits "will work with mayors and councils to identify barriers holding places back", but the Conservatives have described the office as a "gimmick".

There will be no redundancies elsewehere in the civil service as a result of the hiring spree, the BBC has been told, with some jobs expected to be relocated and other vacant roles closed.

The new roles, all based in Manchester, cover areas including strategy, communications, engagement, private office and policy.

BBC News has calculated they total up to £2.8m for basic salaries alone, excluding employer pension contributions in the civil service of 28.97%.

No10 North now has 120 members of staff, nearly half of the 280 staff who work in No10 London.

Among the highest paid of the roles are a "rewiring the state deputy director", with a salary band of £86,000 to £117,000, who will "lead the Rewiring the State Unit... shaping the government's approach to devolution across departments".

The government said it was launching a recruitment campaign for staff who would "bring fresh perspectives and knowledge of the places they serve, moving decisions closer to the people they affect".

No10 North "is driving the most significant transfer of power out of Westminster in a generation," the government added in a statement.

Some apprenticeships and secondments are also being advertised.

It comes as the government confirmed on Friday that No10 North would move from its current temporary home in Heron House, on Manchester's Albert Square, to a new government office on First Street in spring 2027.

No10 North will share the city centre building with other government departments spanning business, education, local government and the Cabinet Office.

Burnham made opening No10 North one of his first acts as prime minister , describing it as "the nerve-centre of a rewired Britain" that would help bring growth to more areas of Britain.

No10 North's deputy director Duncan Parish said in a speech last week that officials faced "institutional challenges" with delivering on these aims and called for a "mindset shift" across the UK's central government.

Conservative Party deputy leader Alex Burghart said: "He [Burnham] promised to streamline the civil service, but now he is hiring extra staff and, once again, won't say where the money is coming from.

"Manchesterism is just more bureaucracy at taxpayers' expense."

Meanwhile, Tory shadow cabinet minister Mike Wood has said there is "so little transparency" around No10 North after ministers told him they could not reveal figures on headcounts and office attendance.

According to the new job adverts, the Office for the Prime Minister - with exceptions for certain roles - expects No10 staff to be in the office a minimum of 60% of the time.

Since opening, No10 North has hosted summits of regional mayors, at least two of which have been partly held as video calls on Microsoft Teams. At one of these meetings, ministers unveiled controversial powers for mayors in England to charge new fees on visitors' overnight stays.

It has also hosted an education summit of school leaders and Irish Taoiseach Micheál Martin met Burnham for the first time as PM at No10 North in September.

articles.title: Uttarakhand chopper flying: A lot has changed for better, but a lot remains to be done
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Hours after seven people on board an Aryan Aviation chopper died when it crashed near Gaurikund on June 15, 2025, the aviation ministry had
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Hours after seven people on board an Aryan Aviation chopper died when it crashed near Gaurikund on June 15, 2025, the aviation ministry had found two helicopters of Trans Bharat — whose chopper crashed on Friday — were airborne “under unsuitable weather conditions.” It had suspended the licences of both Trans Bharat pilots for six months.While the cause of Trans Bharat’s Friday crash in which six people lost their lives will be known once the inquiry report is out, there have been red flags regarding this and several other chopper operators in the hill region. The Uttarakhand govt has grounded Trans Bharat fleet for now.Aviation industry insiders point out that six days before Friday crash, another Trans Bharat helicopter carrying five pilgrims from Sahastradhara to Kedarnath via Guptkashi had made an emergency landing at Baurari stadium on Oct 24 “where children were playing.” Luckily all six, five passengers and the pilot, were safe that day and the chopper took off soon again.“On May 20, 2026, a Trans Bharat Bell 407 flying from Badrinath to Dehradun with seven people on board ran into severe downdrafts over the Chamba–Arakot sector of Tehri Garhwal. During the emergency landing that followed, its tail struck a 33 kV high-tension line. The pilot, a former IAF pilot, got everyone down uninjured,” said sources. Uttarakhand Civil Aviation Development Authority (UCADA) is probing this case.The Char Dham corridor has no single agency answerable for safety. While the DGCA licenses the operators and pilots, UCADA runs the helipads, sets slots and manages shuttle operations. The Sanjay Kumar Jha-headed parliamentary standing committee on transport, tourism and culture had in Aug 2025 called this arrangement “inherently unsafe and unsustainable.” It said there was a “responsibility vacuum” between the two agencies. It found that the DGCA was acting as a passive licensing authority. It also noted that India still has no mandatory, terrain-specific mountain-flying training or certification for pilots operating in the Himalaya.This changed significantly after last summer following a spate of chopper crashes in Uttarakhand. Air traffic control units are being set up, with Kedarnath having one now and Badrinath to get a unti soon. Routes have been defined in the region and take offs are both restricted in number and controlled in a defined pattern with some gap. This is a far cry from the almost unregulated chopper movement in the hill region till last summer.“System wise there has been a lot of improvement. The Char Dham Operations are quite extensive in every aspect. From commercial to maintenance and from operations to ATC, every department is working very hard to ensure safety and efficiency is achieved. After the season of 2025 , there are many different measures that are implemented to ensure highest safety standards are met. These include ATC at Sahastradhara and Sitapur to ensure that flying is well coordinated and controlled,” said Captain Nitin Welde, a senior chopper pilot who operates in Uttarakhand.“There’s a fuel bowser at Sahastradhara to ensure that IOCL supplies fuel in best possible manner. Take off and landing tarmac is separated from parking Tarmac to ensure orderly flow of positioning. There are CCTV cameras all across valley which give feed through a mobile app. All can get a live feed as regards weather valley. For higher helipads above 10,000 feet, the weight limitations are in place and that ensures higher reserve of power while landing and take off. Training for pilots has increased since last year. And there is adequate training in Char Dham sector as well as Kedar shuttles. The DGCA FOIs have been visiting the valley on a weekly basis and UCADA ops department is fully involved in a minute to minute monitoring and support,” added Captain Welde.“Friday was a sad day where it appears that weather in exit phase of Badri valley wasn’t good,” Captain Welde said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Oil-covered debris travelled more than 5,000 miles from Brazil to Florida, revealing how plastic can carry pollution across oceans
articles.summary: Oil-covered plastic bottles, glass containers and rubber fragments found on Florida beaches in 2020 have been traced to a major oil spill off Brazil's
articles.body: Oil-covered plastic bottles, glass containers and rubber fragments found on Florida beaches in 2020 have been traced to a major oil spill off Brazil's coastline in 2019, revealing how marine debris can carry pollution across entire ocean basins. Scientists from Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution and Northeastern University found that petroleum residues travelled approximately 8,500 kilometres (more than 5,000 miles) over 240 days before reaching Florida. According to the study published in Environmental Science & Technology, titled ‘Long-Range Transport of Oil by Marine Plastic Debris: Evidence from an 8500 km Journey’, ocean-current modelling and chemical fingerprinting to establish the connection, highlighting how floating plastic waste can extend the reach of oil pollution far beyond its source.How did oil-covered debris reach Florida beaches from thousands of miles awayThe investigation began when members of Friends of Palm Beach, a non-profit organisation involved in cleaning Florida's coastline, noticed an unusual increase in debris covered with black residue. From late May through September 2020, volunteers found plastic and glass bottles, along with large rubber fragments, arriving on beaches in Palm Beach. The bottles carried labels in Portuguese, Spanish and English, with some identified as consumer products from South American and Caribbean countries. The researchers noted that there was no known local oil spill during the period under investigation.The scale and persistence of the discovery made the incident unusual. According to the research paper, between 10 and 12 residue-coated items were removed during daily beach clean-ups at the height of the event in June and July 2020. The number subsequently declined to between one and three items by mid-September. Friends of Palm Beach shared photographs and observations of the debris online, attracting the attention of researchers. The organisation's observations became an important starting point for the investigation, allowing scientists to examine an environmental event that might otherwise have remained unexplained.Scientists trace Florida's oil-covered debris to Brazil's 2019 oil spillThe researchers investigated whether the petroleum residues could have originated from an oil spill that affected more than 3,000 kilometres of Brazil's coastline between August and December 2019. The incident was described in the study as the worst oil spill in Brazil's history. Oil contamination had been reported along the country's coastline, but its precise source remained unresolved. The researchers considered whether some of the petroleum had attached itself to floating marine debris and travelled towards Florida through ocean currents.To investigate the possibility, the team used ocean-current simulations to reconstruct potential routes taken by floating objects before they reached Florida. The researchers also examined historical drift-bottle experiments conducted in the Western Tropical Atlantic and Caribbean Sea. These experiments had previously recorded bottles released north of northeastern Brazil reaching southeastern Florida after travelling between 4,600 and 5,700 kilometres. The combined modelling and historical observations supported the possibility of long-distance transport. The researchers estimated that the journey from Brazil to Florida took approximately 240 days, consistent with the timing of the two pollution events.Chemical tests link Florida's oil-covered debris to Brazil's 2019 oil spillOcean-current modelling alone could not establish the origin of the black residue. Researchers therefore conducted detailed chemical analyses of samples collected from the Florida debris and compared them with oil samples previously obtained from Brazil's 2019 spill. The investigation used several techniques, including gas chromatography, mass spectrometry and petroleum biomarker analysis. These methods allowed the team to compare the chemical composition of the residues and identify similarities between the samples.The results showed that several Florida samples matched the Brazilian oil samples. In particular, samples labelled FOPB-01, FOPB-02, FOPB-05, FOPB-08 and FOPB-09 showed evidence linking them to the 2019 spill. However, the researchers did not find that every sample had the same origin. FOPB-03 had a different chemical composition and was considered unlikely to have come from the Brazilian spill. The chemical findings, combined with the oceanographic evidence, provided the researchers with evidence that petroleum residues had travelled across the Atlantic while attached to floating debris.What is petroplastic, and how can it transport oil pollution across oceansThe findings highlight the interaction between plastic waste and petroleum contamination in the marine environment. Oil released into the ocean generally undergoes weathering through processes such as evaporation, dissolution, sunlight exposure and microbial activity. These processes usually limit how far spilt oil can travel. However, when petroleum residues attach themselves to floating plastic and other debris, they may remain in the marine environment for longer and move across much greater distances.WHOI chemical oceanographer Christopher Reddy described the process as an additive contaminant effect. In the institution's January 2026 announcement, he said: “Plastic doesn't just pollute on its own—it can act as a vehicle for oil, transporting petroleum contamination across oceans.” The researchers used the term “petroplastic” to describe this interaction between plastic pollution and petroleum contamination. Their study demonstrates how debris originating in one region can carry pollutants into another, creating environmental consequences beyond the location of the original spill. The researchers also noted that further investigation is needed to understand how floating debris protects attached oil from the processes that normally break it down.The study, Evidence from an 8500 km Journey, was led by Bryan D. James and published in Environmental Science & Technology, volume 60, pages 2649–2661. It concluded that floating marine debris can facilitate the long-distance movement of oil pollution, demonstrating how contamination originating in one part of the ocean can have consequences across national and regional boundaries.You use AI every day. Calendar invites determine which children see their father on which days. Each unit has its own schedule, its own nanny team, and its own relationship to the central calendar. The units do not frequently interact with each other despite sharing a father. The half siblings exist in parallel rather than in community,” the post alleged.Replying to the post, Elon Musk clarified “This is wrong on many levels. My older 5 children are adults and live independent lives.”“I see my kids with Claire every other week and kids with Shivon every few days. That’s the whole schedule,” Musk further stated.Elon Musk has 14 children with four womenElon Musk has 14 publicly known children with four women: his first wife, Canadian author Justine Wilson; musician Grimes, whose real name is Claire Boucher; Neuralink executive Shivon Zilis; and conservative influencer and author Ashley St. Clair. articles.title: 'Europeans balked': G20 foreign ministers' meeting opens without group photo. Here's why
articles.summary: Foreign ministers of the G20 largest economies began a two-day meeting in the US on Friday (local time), with the gathering notably skipping the customary
articles.body: Foreign ministers of the G20 largest economies began a two-day meeting in the US on Friday (local time), with the gathering notably skipping the customary group photograph.According to reports, US secretary of state Marco Rubio cancelled the traditional group photo after several European officials threatened to boycott or walk out over Russia's participation. Moscow is being represented by foreign minister Sergei Lavrov at the summit in Atlanta.Two US officials told The Associated Press that European officials "balked" at the prospect of being photographed with Lavrov, prompting Rubio to cancel the picture to avoid what could possibly become a “distraction.”Several G20 countries had already raised concerns over the US inviting Russia despite Moscow's war against Ukraine, which began in February 2022.In a statement, the British Foreign Office reiterated the UK's longstanding policy of avoiding direct bilateral engagement with Russian ministers over the war in Ukraine, adding that it had "no plans" to change its stance.Polish deputy Prime Minister Radosław Sikorski, who is also the country's foreign minister, called the cancellation of the group photograph “the right decision.” Speaking to the media, he remarked: “I am not the only one who does not want to be photographed with Lavrov.”German top diplomat Johann Wadephul stressed that “there is no normality with Russia”, but added that differences must be asserted at the negotiating table. He also cautioned against sending “falsely optimistic signals."Lavrov has made only occasional visits to Nato member states since the Russia-Ukraine war began and Western sanctions were subsequently imposed on Moscow.'We are in a critical moment': RubioRubio opened the talks, which otherwise proceeded as planned, with an appeal for unity on issues threatening international security and global trade.“We are in a critical moment — I would call it a moment of choosing, and I would say not just for my country, the United States of America, but frankly, for the world,” Rubio told his counterparts.“We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises,” he added, citing disruptions to global energy and food supplies, trade and freedom of navigation. He warned that many of these developments posed “severe threats to essential foundations of the global economic order."However, there were not many signs of consensus among G20 diplomats on several contentious issues, including the Russia-Ukraine conflict, the US-Israeli war against Iran, US tariffs and China's actions in the South China Sea. These tensions have contributed to rising global fuel costs and growing uncertainty over trade.The Atlanta meeting is intended to lay the groundwork for the G20 leaders' summit, which US President Donald Trump is scheduled to host at his Miami golf club in December. It remains unclear whether Russian President Vladimir Putin will accept Trump's invitation to attend.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
